title: Code review: responding to and giving review
summary: How review decides whether a change lands: the code-health standard, answering every comment, writing clear labeled comments, GitHub review mechanics, why response time dominates, and mailing-list review.
outcomes: Explain Google's review standard: approve once a change definitely improves code health, even if imperfect
Respond to every review comment by fixing code, clarifying it, reasoning through disagreement, or filing a follow-up
Write review comments that target the code, explain why, and label severity such as Nit: or non-blocking
Predict when GitHub's Request changes, required reviews, stale dismissal and suggestion batching affect a PR
Compute how reviewer response time multiplies across review rounds, and use Reviewed-by and Tested-by tags correctly

lessons.title: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard

blocks.md: In the previous course you opened a pull request (PR): a small, focused change with a description that explains what it does and why. Opening it is not the end. Before it lands, at least one other person reads the diff, asks questions and asks for changes, and you answer and update the code. That back-and-forth is **code review**, and it decides whether your change is merged, reworked or closed.

Two naive views of review both fail. If the reviewer treats review as a gate for perfection, every PR takes weeks and people stop sending improvements at all. If the reviewer treats it as a rubber stamp, small shortcuts pile up and the codebase slowly degrades. Google's published review guide says exactly this: codebases usually get worse through many small decreases in quality, often under time pressure.

blocks.title: One review round trip on a typical PR

scenes.caption: The author opens the PR. CI (continuous integration) runs the test suite automatically, so the human reviewer does not have to check what a machine can.
The reviewer reads the diff, leaves line comments and submits a review. Here the decision is Request changes: one comment must be addressed before merging.
The author answers every comment, pushes a fix commit and asks for another look. CI runs again on the new commit.
The reviewer checks only what changed since the last round, approves, and a maintainer with merge rights lands it. Every extra round trip adds another wait.

blocks.md: So what should the reviewer be deciding? Google's engineering practices guide (published as open source) states the senior rule of its whole review process: reviewers should favor approving a change once it **definitely improves the overall code health** of the system, even if it is not perfect. *Code health* means how maintainable, readable and understandable the code is, plus its correctness.
Approve when the change makes the codebase better than it was, not when it matches what you would have written. There is no perfect code, only better code. The goal is continuous improvement.

The rule has limits. A reviewer may refuse a well-built feature the project does not want, and nothing justifies merging a change that clearly makes code health worse, except in an emergency. When opinions collide, Google's guide orders the arguments: technical facts and data beat opinions; the project's style guide is the authority on style; design questions are judged on engineering principles; and if several approaches are equally valid, the author's choice wins.

A practical consequence: comments now come in two kinds. Some are required for the change to improve the code. Others are polish the author could skip. The guide asks reviewers to mark the second kind, for example with a `Nit:` prefix (short for nitpick), so the author knows they can ignore it. You will see this convention throughout the rest of the course.
Misconception: a reviewer who leaves 15 comments is blocking you on all 15. Often most are optional. If the reviewer did not say which ones block the merge, ask instead of guessing.

blocks.question: A PR fixes a real bug and adds a test, but the reviewer would have named one helper function differently and prefers a slightly different loop style that the style guide does not mention. Under Google's standard, what should the reviewer do?
options: Request changes until both points are fixed, since the PR is not yet perfect
Approve, optionally leaving the naming and loop points as Nit: comments
Close the PR and write the fix themselves in their preferred style
Approve only after a third reviewer agrees on the naming
blocks.explain: The change definitely improves code health (a fixed bug plus a test). Style points not in the style guide are personal preference, so they should not block. Marking them Nit: keeps the feedback without delaying the merge.

blocks.question: Which situation lets a reviewer withhold approval even if the code is clean and well tested?
options: The reviewer would have used a different but equally valid algorithm
The author used tabs where the style guide is silent and the file already uses tabs
The PR adds a feature the project has decided it does not want
The PR is 40 lines and the reviewer expected 30
blocks.explain: Google's guide explicitly allows denying a feature the maintainers do not want in their system, however well designed. An equally valid alternative should defer to the author, consistency with the existing file is correct, and line counts alone are not a reason.

lessons.title: Answering review comments as the author

blocks.md: Now take the author's seat. A reviewer left five comments on your PR. The Linux kernel's patch guide is blunt about the first rule: you must respond to review comments, because ignoring reviewers is a good way to get ignored in return. Respond to **every** comment, including the ones you disagree with and the optional ones you decide to skip.

Each comment ends in one of a few states. You change the code. You reply with a clarification or a reasoned disagreement. Or, if the request is valid but outside this PR's scope, you open a follow-up issue and link it, which GitHub's docs describe as the way to track out-of-scope suggestions. The tracker below follows five comments through one round.

blocks.title: Tracking five review comments through one round

scenes.caption: Five comments arrive: a real bug (C1), a question because the reviewer could not follow some code (C2), a design disagreement (C3), a Nit (C4), and a request for a larger refactor (C5). All start open.
C1 is a clear bug: fix it in code and reply saying what changed. C4 is optional but cheap, so take it. Both become fixed.
C2: the reviewer did not understand the code, so future readers will not either. Rename and restructure it, or add a code comment, rather than only explaining in the thread.
C3: you disagree. Reply with your tradeoffs and ask which tradeoff the reviewer weighs differently. It stays open until you reach consensus.
C5 is valid but out of scope. Open an issue, link it in the reply, and keep this PR focused. Every comment now has a visible answer.

blocks.md: The C2 rule comes from Google's guide for authors: if a reviewer says they do not understand something, your first response should be to **clarify the code itself**. If the code cannot be clarified, add a code comment that explains why it is there. Only when a comment seems pointless should the answer live in the review thread alone. A reply in the review tool helps one reader once; clearer code helps every future reader.

blocks.prompt: A reviewer asks: "Why do we retry 3 times here?" You know the answer (an upstream API is flaky). Where should the answer go?
blocks.reveal: **Into the code**, as a named constant or a short comment such as `# upstream API intermittently drops calls, so retry up to 3 times`, plus a one-line reply pointing to it. The kernel guide says the same: review questions that do not lead to a code change should almost certainly lead to a code comment or changelog entry, so the next reviewer understands.

blocks.md: For disagreements, Google's guide contrasts two replies. Bad: "No, I'm not going to do that." Good: state why you chose X with its pros, cons and tradeoffs, say why you think Y is worse, and ask whether the reviewer thinks Y better serves those tradeoffs, weighs them differently, or means something else. You may know something about the users or code that the reviewer does not; give them that context.

blocks.code:
Thanks for the careful read!

C1: Good catch, the off-by-one is fixed in 3f2a9c1 and covered by
    test_empty_batch.
C2: Renamed `proc2` to `drop_expired_entries` and added a comment
    on why we scan in reverse.
C3: I kept the linear scan: the list is capped at 64 entries, so a
    heap adds code without a measurable win (benchmark in the PR
    description). Do you weigh readability differently here?
C4: Done.
C5: Agreed this is worth doing; opened #418 to track it so this PR
    stays focused.
blocks.caption: A reply that answers every comment, says what changed and where, and thanks the reviewer.

blocks.md: Never reply in anger. Google's guide calls it a serious breach of etiquette that lives forever in the review tool. If a comment stings, ask what constructive point the reviewer is making, and answer that point once you are calm.

Answer every comment, say what you changed, fix the code rather than explaining it in the thread, and thank the reviewer. The kernel guide adds: when you send a new version, list what changed since the previous one.

blocks.question: A reviewer writes: "I can't tell what this regex is matching." Which response best follows the guidance in this lesson?
options: Reply in the thread with a full explanation of the regex
Resolve the conversation, since it is a question and not a change request
Ask the reviewer to read the regex documentation
Split the regex into named parts or add a comment explaining what it matches, then reply pointing to it
blocks.explain: If the reviewer cannot follow the code, future readers will not either. Clarifying the code (or adding a comment when it cannot be simpler) fixes the problem for everyone. A thread reply only helps this one reviewer, and silently resolving leaves the question unanswered.

blocks.question: A reviewer asks you to also refactor an unrelated module your PR happens to call. The request is reasonable but would double the PR's size. What is the best move?
options: Do the refactor in this PR so the reviewer approves
Explain it is out of scope, open an issue to track it, and link the issue in your reply
Ignore the comment since it is not about your change
Close the PR and start over with both changes
blocks.explain: Ignoring a comment is the one thing every guide warns against. Folding unrelated work in makes the PR harder to review. GitHub's docs suggest opening an issue for out-of-scope feedback, which keeps the PR focused and the suggestion from getting lost.

lessons.title: Giving review: reading order and comments that land

blocks.md: Now switch seats. You are reviewing someone else's PR. Two questions: in what order do you read it, and how do you phrase what you find? Google's guide on navigating a change gives a three-step order, and the reason for it is time: a major design problem can make most of the other line comments pointless.

blocks.title: An efficient order for reading a PR

nodes.label:
Read description:
does this make sense?

Say no early,
suggest an alternative

Main file:
is the design sound?

scenes.caption: Step one: read the description and the change as a whole. If this change should not happen at all, say so immediately, politely, and suggest what to do instead.
Step two: find the main part, often the file with the most logical changes, and judge its design first. It gives context for every smaller file.
If the design has a major problem, send those comments right away, before reading the rest. The author may already be building on this design, and big rework takes longest.
Only when the design is sound, read the remaining files in a sensible order. Reading the tests first can tell you what the change is meant to do. Then submit one review with a summary.

blocks.md: While reading, Google's checklist covers design, functionality (edge cases, concurrency), complexity (including over-engineering for imagined future needs), tests that would actually fail if the code broke, naming, comments that explain *why* rather than *what*, and style. You do not need to repeat what CI already checks.

Then, how to write the comment. Google's guide summarizes it in four points: be kind; explain your reasoning; balance pointing out problems with giving direct instructions; and encourage simpler code or code comments over explanations to you. Comment on the **code**, never on the developer.

blocks.prompt: Which comment would you rather receive? (a) "Why did you use threads here when there's obviously no benefit from concurrency?" (b) "The concurrency model here adds complexity without a performance benefit I can see, so this code is best single-threaded."
blocks.reveal: Almost everyone picks **(b)**, and it is Google's own good example. It talks about the code, not the person ("you", "obviously"), and it explains *why*, so the author can either agree or bring data showing a benefit. The technical content of the two comments is identical; only the framing changed.

blocks.md: **Label severity.** Without labels, authors tend to treat every comment as mandatory. Google suggests prefixes such as `Nit:` (minor, would be nice), `Optional:` or `Consider:` (good idea, not required) and `FYI:` (not for this PR). The Conventional Comments format generalizes this as `label (decorations): subject`, with labels like `praise`, `nitpick`, `suggestion`, `issue`, `question` and `thought`, and decorations such as `(blocking)` or `(non-blocking)`.

blocks.title: Same six comments, how many look mandatory?

scenes.caption: Simplified example: a review with 6 comments, of which 2 are real issues and 4 are polish. With no labels, a careful author may treat all 6 as required.
With labels (issue: twice, nitpick: or Optional: four times) the author can see that only 2 block the merge and do those first. The reviewer's intent is now explicit.

blocks.code:
issue (blocking): `limit` can be 0 here, which makes the loop
below run forever. Could we return early when limit <= 0?

nitpick (non-blocking): `cnt` reads better as `count`.

question: Is this cache shared across threads? If so, the
read-modify-write on line 42 needs a lock.

praise: Splitting the parser out made this much easier to test.
blocks.caption: Conventional Comments style: the label and decoration say how much each comment matters before the reader gets to the content.

blocks.md: Two more habits from the guide. Point out what is good, too, with the reason, because people learn from reinforcement. And you do not have to design the fix: it is the author's job to fix the change, and pointing out the problem often leads to a better solution because the author is closer to the code. Give direct code when it is clearly more helpful.

When you ask the author to explain code you do not understand, the answer should usually be clearer code or, occasionally, a code comment. An explanation that only lives in the review thread does not help future readers; accept one only when normal readers of that code would already know it.

blocks.question: You are reviewing a 600-line PR. In the main file you find the data model is wrong, which will force most other files to change. You have only 20 minutes now. What should you do?
options: Finish leaving line comments on every other file first so the review is complete
Approve with a note that the design should be revisited later
Wait until you have time to review all 600 lines in one sitting
Send the design comment immediately, saying you will review the rest once the design is settled
blocks.explain: Google's guide says to send major design comments right away: much of the remaining code will change anyway, and the author may already be building on this design. Line comments on code that will be rewritten waste both people's time. Approving a known-wrong design worsens code health.

blocks.question: Which comment is phrased the way this lesson recommends?
options: "You clearly didn't test this."
"Nit: this could be a list comprehension, but the loop is fine too."
"This is wrong."
"Why would anyone write it like this?"
blocks.explain: It is labeled (Nit: tells the author it is optional), it is about the code, and it says the existing version is acceptable. The others aim at the person or give no reason and no way forward.

lessons.title: GitHub mechanics: decisions, suggestions and merge rules

blocks.md: Everything so far is tool-independent. On GitHub, the mechanics shape how the conversation flows, and a few details surprise newcomers. A **review** on GitHub is a batch of line comments plus one decision. GitHub's docs list three decisions: **Comment** (general feedback, no verdict), **Approve** (ready to merge) and **Request changes** (feedback the author should address before merging).

When you click Start a review, your line comments are **pending**: only you can see them, and you can edit or discard them. They are published together when you submit the review with a summary. GitHub notes that batching avoids sending a notification for every comment, which is one reason to review in one pass instead of posting comments one by one.

blocks.title: From pending comments to a merge on GitHub

scenes.caption: Line comments start as pending drafts. Submitting publishes them all at once with a summary and one decision.
The decision matters only through branch rules. GitHub's docs: Request changes is purely informational unless a ruleset or branch protection requires a pull request with reviews.
With required reviews on, a write-access reviewer's Request changes blocks merging until that same person submits an approving review. Authors can never approve their own PR.
If stale review dismissal is also enabled, pushing a code-modifying commit dismisses existing approvals and the PR needs a fresh approval. Expect a re-review after late changes.

blocks.md: The most useful GitHub feature for small fixes is the **suggestion**. In a line comment, a code block fenced with the word `suggestion` proposes an exact replacement for the selected line or lines. Select multiple lines by dragging from the first to the last line number, then click Make a Suggestion; GitHub copies those lines into the block for you to edit. You can write an explanation above the block.

blocks.code:
Off-by-one: `n` is the last valid index here, so range(0, n, 2)
skips it when n is even.

```suggestion
    for i in range(0, n + 1, 2):
```
blocks.caption: A review comment with a suggestion block. The author can click Commit suggestion to apply it.

blocks.md: On the author's side, GitHub's docs describe two options: **Commit suggestion** applies one suggestion as its own commit, and **Add suggestion to batch** collects several so that Commit suggestions applies them all as a single commit. Each person whose suggestion is included becomes a co-author of that commit. Applying requires write access to the repository (or, for a fork PR, a maintainer with write access upstream when edits from maintainers are allowed).

blocks.prompt: A reviewer left 6 one-line suggestions. You click Commit suggestion on each one separately. What does the PR history look like, and what would batching change?
blocks.reveal: Six separate commits on the PR branch (and, in a typical CI setup, six CI runs). Batching (Add suggestion to batch, then Commit suggestions) produces **one** commit with every suggester credited as co-author. Either way, read each suggestion first: it is code you are signing up to own.

blocks.md: Two last mechanics. **Resolve conversation** collapses a finished thread so open ones are easy to find; the PR author and anyone with write access can do it. And after substantial changes, use the re-request review button so the reviewer is notified that it is their turn again.

Do not resolve a reviewer's thread you disagreed with and did not change. Collapsing a thread hides it from the list of open conversations, so silently resolving an open disagreement reads as ignoring it. Reply, and resolve only when the thread is truly finished.

blocks.question: A repository has no branch protection or rulesets. A maintainer submits Request changes on your PR. Can someone with merge rights still merge it?
options: No, Request changes always blocks merging until the reviewer approves
Yes, without a rule requiring reviews, Request changes is informational
No, GitHub requires at least two approvals by default
Only after the reviewer dismisses their own review
blocks.explain: GitHub's docs say Request changes is purely informational unless a ruleset or classic branch protection rule requires pull request reviews. The social signal still matters: merging over an unresolved request is a team decision, not a tool one.

blocks.question: Your PR was approved, then you pushed one more commit fixing a typo in code. The repository requires reviews and has stale review dismissal on. What happens?
options: The approval stays because the change was small
The PR merges automatically
The approval is dismissed and the PR needs a new approval before merging
GitHub reverts your commit
blocks.explain: With required reviews and stale review dismissal enabled, any code-modifying commit pushed to an approved PR dismisses the approval. GitHub does not judge whether the change was small.

lessons.title: Why reviewer response time dominates time to merge

blocks.md: Review quality is not the only thing that matters; so does speed. Google's guide optimizes for the speed of the team, not of one developer, and sets a clear bar: **one business day is the maximum time to respond** to a review request. It stresses *response time* (how long each reply takes), not the time until merge, and says not to interrupt focused work to review; wait for a natural break.

Why does response time dominate? Because a PR with several rounds pays the reviewer's wait on every round. Here is a simple model in working hours. Let $n$ be the number of fix rounds, $R$ the reviewer's response time and $F$ the time the author takes to fix comments. The reviewer is waited on $n+1$ times (the first look plus one re-review after each fix):

blocks.caption: Simplified model: ignores time zones, CI time and the reviewer's own reading time.

blocks.md: Take $n = 2$ fix rounds and $F = 2$ hours per fix. A reviewer who responds within $R = 2$ hours gives $3 \times 2 + 2 \times 2 = 10$ hours. A reviewer who always takes the maximum one business day ($R = 8$ working hours) gives $3 \times 8 + 2 \times 2 = 28$ hours, or 3.5 working days, for the same work.

blocks.title: Same PR, two reviewer response times (working hours)

scenes.caption: Fast reviewer (R = 2 h): three short waits and two 2 h fixes. Merged after 10 working hours, within about one and a quarter days.
Slow reviewer (R = 8 h, one business day each time). The author's work is identical, but the PR takes 28 working hours. Waiting is 24 of those 28 hours.
Same slow reviewer, but at round 2 only minor comments remain, so they approve with comments (LGTM with comments). The third wait disappears: 20 hours.

blocks.md: **LGTM with comments** (LGTM means "looks good to me") is Google's name for approving while leaving unresolved comments. The guide allows it when the reviewer trusts the author to address the rest, when the remaining comments are optional, or when they are minor (sort imports, fix a typo, apply a suggested fix). It is especially useful across time zones, where one more round can cost a full day.

blocks.title: Total review time vs reviewer response time

scenes.caption: With n = 2 and F = 2, each hour of reviewer response time adds 3 hours to the total, because it is paid on 3 rounds. The marked points are the 10 h and 28 h cases above.
Raise n to 4 rounds: the slope becomes 5. Many rounds make slow responses much worse, which is why small PRs that need fewer rounds and fast replies go together.
With n = 0 (approved on first look), total time is just R. The model also shows the author's side: F is paid n times, so prompt fixes matter too.

blocks.md: Real data supports the shape of this model. A 2018 study of about 9 million reviewed changes at Google (Sadowski et al., *Modern Code Review: A Case Study at Google*) found the median change touches 24 lines, has 1 reviewer, and more than 80% of changes need at most one iteration of resolving comments. The median wait for first feedback was under an hour for small changes and about 5 hours for very large ones.

blocks.title: Median review time reported in the Google study

scenes.caption: Median hours to approval reported by Rigby and Bird, as cited in the Google paper. The Google bar is drawn at 4 h, an upper bound: the paper reports its median for the whole review process as under 4 hours.

The paper links Google's speed to small changes (median 24 lines) and usually one reviewer. Different companies measured slightly different endpoints, so read this as a contrast in scale, not an exact ranking.

blocks.md: Fast does not mean shallow. Google's guide says reviewers must spend enough time that their approval really means the code meets the standard, and that if a change is too large to review quickly, the right response is to ask for it to be split into smaller changes, or at least send early comments on the overall design.

blocks.question: Using the model with n = 2 and F = 2, a reviewer who used to take 8 hours per response now takes 4. How much does total time to merge drop?
options: From 28 h to 24 h
From 28 h to 16 h
From 28 h to 14 h
It does not change, since the author's work is the same
blocks.explain: Total is (n+1)R + nF. Before: 3 x 8 + 4 = 28 h. After: 3 x 4 + 4 = 16 h. Each hour saved per response is saved on all three rounds, so 4 hours faster per response saves 12 hours in total.

blocks.question: A reviewer in another time zone sees that only two typo fixes remain. The author will be asleep for the next 10 hours. What does Google's guide suggest?
options: Request changes so the author fixes the typos, then review again tomorrow
Wait to approve until the typos are fixed, to keep the process strict
Approve with comments (LGTM with comments), noting the typos to fix before merging
Fix the typos and approve your own commit
blocks.explain: Minor remaining comments are exactly the case for LGTM with comments, and the guide calls it especially worth considering across time zones. Requesting another round costs the author a full extra day for two typos.

lessons.title: Review by email: patch versions and trailer tags

blocks.md: Not every open source project reviews on GitHub. The Linux kernel and several other projects review **patches by email** on public mailing lists. The principles are the same, but the mechanics are explicit and worth knowing: version numbers in the subject, a changelog of what changed between versions, and **trailers** (tag lines at the end of the commit message) that record who reviewed and tested a patch.

blocks.title: A patch through three versions on a mailing list

scenes.caption: The author mails [PATCH] to the list. Reviewers reply inline, interleaving their comments with quoted lines of the patch. The kernel docs strongly discourage top-posting.
The author replies to each comment, says what will change and thanks the reviewer. Then sends v2, with what changed since v1 written below the --- line.
A tester replies with Tested-by:, the reviewer with Reviewed-by:. The author adds both tags to the patch when sending the next version.

v3 changes the error path substantially, so the old Tested-by may no longer apply: the author drops it and says why in the changelog. Rita re-checked v3 and confirmed her Reviewed-by, so it stays. The maintainer applies it.

blocks.md: The version changelog is the email equivalent of a reply that lists what changed. The kernel guide asks you to put it **after the `---` marker line**. Everything above that line becomes the permanent commit message; the notes between that line and the diff are for reviewers only and are stripped automatically when the patch is applied. Links to earlier versions on lore.kernel.org help reviewers too.

blocks.code:
Subject: [PATCH v3] net: foo: fix refcount leak on probe error

<commit message explaining the problem and the fix>

Reviewed-by: Rita Reviewer <rita@example.org>
Signed-off-by: Ana Author <ana@example.org>
---
Changes since v2:
 - Moved the cleanup into a helper (Rita)
 - Dropped Tested-by from Tom: the error path changed substantially
Changes since v1:
 - Fixed the leak on the second error path too
v2: https://lore.kernel.org/...
v1: https://lore.kernel.org/...
blocks.caption: Simplified layout of a v3 patch email. The lines below --- are reviewer notes and never reach the git history.

blocks.md:
What the trailers mean, per the kernel guide:

- **Reviewed-by:** the reviewer carried out a technical review, communicated any concerns, is satisfied with the answers, and believes the patch is worthwhile and free of known issues. It is a statement of opinion, not a guarantee.
- **Tested-by:** the person successfully tested the patch in some environment.
- **Acked-by:** less formal; someone responsible for or involved with the code (often a maintainer) agrees with it landing, without necessarily reviewing it as thoroughly.

You may not add a Reviewed-by, Tested-by or Acked-by tag for someone just because they said nice things. The kernel guide says these need the named person's explicit permission; only Cc:, Reported-by: and Suggested-by: can be added with implicit permission.

Patience is part of email review too. The kernel guide says to expect comments within a few weeks (typically 2 to 3), to wait at least one week before resubmitting or pinging reviewers, and longer during busy periods like merge windows. Add `RESEND` to the subject only when resending an **unmodified** patch; a changed patch gets a new version number instead.

Whatever the tool, the author's loop is the same: answer every comment, change the code where the reviewer was right, record what changed between versions, and carry earned review credit forward only while it still applies.

blocks.question: Your v2 patch got a Reviewed-by from Rita. For v3 you only reworded a code comment she asked about. For v4 you rewrote the whole locking scheme. Which is right?
options: Keep Reviewed-by in v3 and v4, since tags are permanent once given
Drop it in v3, because any change invalidates review
Keep it in v3, drop it in v4 and say why below the --- line
Drop it in both and add Acked-by instead
blocks.explain: Tags received on the list should be carried into the next versions, but if the patch changes substantially they may no longer apply and should be removed, with the removal explained in the changelog after the --- separator. Converting it to Acked-by without permission would be inventing a tag.

blocks.question: Where should "v1 to v2: renamed helper per review" go in a kernel patch email, and why?
options: Above the Signed-off-by lines, so it is preserved in git history
Below the --- line, because it helps reviewers but is stripped when the patch is applied
In a separate email after the patch
Nowhere; reviewers can diff the versions themselves
blocks.explain: The kernel guide says version history is for reviewers, not the permanent changelog. Below the --- marker it is dropped automatically when the patch is applied; above the tags it would need manual removal.
